# Eligibility verification and prior authorization: workflows and staffing

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** Verify eligibility and benefits before every visit, not just the first. Confirm active coverage, plan type, cost sharing, coordination of benefits, and whether the service needs a referral or prior authorization. Then track each authorization's expiration and visit limits. CMS-0057-F now sets decision timeframes for many payers, but practices still need staff to submit requests and follow up.

Most denials are decided before the patient arrives. If coverage wasn't active, benefits weren't understood, or an authorization was missing, no amount of A/R follow-up will fully fix it. This guide covers eligibility verification and prior authorization, what changed recently in federal rules, the workflows that work, and how practices staff them. It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.

## Why the front end matters

In a 2025 vendor survey of billing professionals, the top denial reasons were coordination of benefits issues (45% of respondents), non-coverage (39%) and prior authorization or referral issues (31%) ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)). Federal transparency data show HealthCare.gov insurers attributed 9% of in-network claim denials in 2023 to lack of prior authorization or referral ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/private-insurance/claims-denials-and-appeals-in-aca-marketplace-plans-in-2023/)). All of these are front-end problems.

## Eligibility verification, step by step

### When to verify

- At scheduling, for new patients and new insurance.
- 24 to 72 hours before every visit, for everyone, since coverage changes.
- At check-in, by confirming card, ID and any changes.

### What to verify

- Active coverage on the date of service
- Plan type and network status for the rendering provider and location
- Copay, deductible (met and remaining), coinsurance, out-of-pocket maximum
- Coordination of benefits: is this plan primary?
- Service-specific limits (visit caps for therapy, for example)
- Referral and prior authorization requirements for the planned service

### How

Use real-time 270/271 eligibility transactions through your practice management system or clearinghouse where available, payer portals for detail, and phone calls when portals don't show what you need. Document what you found, where, and the reference number.

### What to do with the result

- Update demographics and insurance in the system.
- Flag inactive coverage and contact the patient before the visit.
- Give the front desk the patient's estimated responsibility so it can be collected at check-in.
- Trigger the authorization workflow if required.

## Verification of benefits (VOB) in behavioral health

Treatment centers and behavioral health programs often run a deeper VOB: benefits by level of care (detox, residential, partial hospitalization, intensive outpatient, outpatient), authorization and concurrent review requirements, out-of-network benefits and day limits. VOB staff usually work with admissions teams under time pressure. See our [behavioral health billing guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/behavioral-health-billing/).

## Prior authorization, step by step

### The workload

The AMA's survey of 1,000 physicians found practices complete an average of 39 prior authorization requests per physician per week, spending about 13 hours on them, and that 40% of physicians have staff who work exclusively on prior authorizations ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/fixing-prior-auth-nearly-40-prior-authorizations-week-way)).

### The workflow

1. **Identify** services needing authorization by payer and code, using payer lists. Keep a maintained matrix.
2. **Gather documentation:** orders, notes, prior treatments tried, test results.
3. **Submit** through the payer portal, electronic transaction or fax, as the payer requires.
4. **Track** pending requests daily, with a due date for each.
5. **Record** the authorization number, approved units or visits, and the date range in the practice management system so it flows to the claim.
6. **Monitor** expirations and visit counts, and request extensions before they run out.
7. **Handle denials:** request a peer-to-peer review if appropriate, or appeal with additional documentation.

## What changed: the CMS prior authorization rule

The CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule (CMS-0057-F) applies to "impacted payers": Medicare Advantage organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities and qualified health plan issuers on the federally facilitated exchanges ([CMS fact sheet](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/cms-interoperability-and-prior-authorization-final-rule-cms-0057-f)). Key points from CMS:

- **Decision timeframes:** impacted payers, excluding FFE qualified health plans, must send prior authorization decisions within **72 hours** for expedited requests and **seven calendar days** for standard requests.
- **Specific denial reasons:** beginning in 2026, impacted payers must give a specific reason for denied prior authorization requests.
- **Public metrics:** payers must post certain prior authorization metrics annually.
- **Prior Authorization API:** payers must implement an API to support electronic requests and responses, generally by January 1, 2027.
- **Drugs are excluded** from these provisions.

For staff, this means more predictable turnaround from these payers and clearer denial reasons to work from, but the volume of authorizations doesn't go away. Commercial plans outside the rule follow their own contracts and applicable state laws.

## Measuring front-end performance

- Percentage of visits verified before the date of service
- Eligibility-related denials (count and dollars)
- Authorization-related denials
- Average days from authorization request to decision, by payer
- Visits performed without a valid authorization (should be zero)

## Staffing eligibility and prior authorization

Both jobs are detail-heavy, deadline-driven and largely done in portals and on the phone, which makes them a good fit for dedicated staff, local or remote. What matters:

- **Protected time.** Authorization work done "between patients" by front-desk staff tends to slip.
- **Payer knowledge.** A maintained authorization matrix and staff who know each payer's portal.
- **Schedule alignment.** Staff working ahead of your schedule (for example, verifying tomorrow's patients today) and overlapping payer phone hours.
- **Clear handoffs** with the front desk and clinicians for missing documentation.
- **Security.** Access only to scheduling, eligibility and authorization screens needed (minimum necessary), unique logins with MFA, and a signed BAA before access. See our [HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/).

This site is operated by [Alliance Global Solutions](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/), whose remote staff include eligibility, prior authorization and [administrative support](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/administrative/) roles. If front-end work is backing up, request a [free staffing assessment](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/).

## Common front-end mistakes to avoid

- **Checking eligibility only for new patients.** Coverage changes at any time: job changes, plan renewals, Medicaid redeterminations. Re-verify before every visit, or at least whenever the schedule is built.
- **Stopping at "active coverage."** A plan can be active and still deny the service for lack of authorization, a visit limit, a carve-out or out-of-network status. Check benefits for the specific service.
- **Not recording the details.** Note who you spoke with, the reference number, the date and what was confirmed. If the payer later denies the claim, that record supports the appeal.
- **Losing track of expirations.** Authorizations expire and visit counts run out. Put both on a calendar with an owner and a lead time for renewal requests.
- **Treating the front desk as the only line of defense.** Front desk staff juggle phones, check-in and payments. A dedicated verification person or team, working a day or two ahead of the schedule, catches problems before the patient arrives.
- **Ignoring secondary coverage.** Coordination-of-benefits problems were the most commonly reported cause of rising denials in Tebra's 2025 survey of billers ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)). Ask every patient about other coverage and confirm which plan is primary.

## Related guides

- [Denial management basics](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/)
- [VOB and authorizations in behavioral health](https://medicalbillingteam.com/behavioral-health-billing/)
- [Revenue cycle management staffing (main guide)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/)
- [Prior authorization specialist role](https://medicalbillingteam.com/prior-authorization-specialist/)

## FAQ

### What is insurance eligibility verification?

It is confirming, before a visit, that a patient's coverage is active and finding out benefits that affect payment: copay, deductible, coinsurance, plan type, network status, coordination of benefits, and whether a referral or prior authorization is required.

### What is a VOB?

VOB stands for verification of benefits. The term is common in behavioral health and treatment centers, where staff verify detailed benefits for specific levels of care before admission.

### How long do payers have to respond to prior authorization requests?

Under the CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule, impacted payers such as Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care plans (excluding FFE qualified health plans for this provision) must send decisions within 72 hours for expedited requests and seven calendar days for standard requests, beginning in 2026. Commercial plans outside the rule follow their own contracts and state laws.

### How much time do practices spend on prior authorization?

In an AMA survey of 1,000 physicians, practices reported an average of 39 prior authorization requests per physician per week, taking about 13 hours of physician and staff time.

### Can eligibility and prior authorization be done by remote staff?

Yes. Both are largely portal- and phone-based, so remote staff can do them well with access to your scheduling system, payer portals and clear rules, plus HIPAA safeguards such as a BAA, MFA and role-based access.

# Medical billing for behavioral health practices and treatment centers

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** Behavioral health billing is harder than it looks. Practices and treatment centers deal with time-based psychotherapy codes, frequent authorizations and concurrent reviews, benefits that vary by level of care, carved-out behavioral health plans, and extra privacy rules for substance use disorder records under 42 CFR Part 2. Billing staff need training in all of these.

Behavioral health billing looks simple from the outside: a lot of the same few codes. In practice, it's one of the more demanding specialties to bill well. Authorizations and concurrent reviews are frequent, benefits vary by level of care, many plans carve behavioral health out to a separate administrator, and substance use disorder (SUD) records carry their own federal privacy rules. This guide covers what's different and how practices and treatment centers staff the work. It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.

## Who this applies to

- Outpatient mental health practices: psychiatrists, psychologists, therapists, counselors and group practices
- Substance use disorder treatment centers across levels of care
- Intensive outpatient (IOP) and partial hospitalization (PHP) programs
- Residential treatment and detox programs
- Billing companies serving these providers

## What makes behavioral health billing different

### 1. Levels of care and benefits

Treatment centers bill across levels of care, each with its own benefits, authorization rules and documentation expectations. A patient's plan may cover residential care differently from IOP, with day limits or step-down requirements.

### 2. Authorizations and concurrent review

Many behavioral health services require prior authorization, and higher levels of care often require **concurrent review**: periodic clinical updates to the payer to continue authorized days. Missed reviews mean unpaid days. Staff need a tracker with review dates, approved days and the clinical contact for each case.

### 3. Carve-outs

A patient's medical plan may route behavioral health claims and authorizations to a separate behavioral health administrator with a different portal, payer ID and rules. Eligibility checks must identify the right entity.

### 4. Time-based and add-on codes

Psychotherapy codes are typically time-based, with add-on codes for things like interactive complexity or crisis services. Documentation must support the time and the service. Use current CPT guidance from the AMA ([AMA CPT overview](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/cpt/cpt-overview-and-code-approval)) and payer policies; coders and billers should work from the current year's code set.

### 5. Privacy rules beyond HIPAA

- **Psychotherapy notes** receive special protection under the HIPAA Privacy Rule: most uses and disclosures require patient authorization ([HHS, Privacy Rule summary](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/laws-regulations/index.html)). Billing staff generally don't need them and shouldn't have access.
- **42 CFR Part 2** protects records of federally assisted SUD programs. It limits disclosures that would identify someone as having an SUD unless Part 2 permits it, allows a single patient consent for treatment, payment and health care operations, and restricts use of records in legal proceedings against patients. HHS notes the 2024 final rule's compliance date was February 16, 2026, and that some Part 2 requirements also apply to recipients such as HIPAA covered entities, business associates and qualified service organizations ([HHS, Part 2](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/hipaa-part-2/index.html)).

Make sure anyone touching Part 2 records, including billing staff, is trained on these rules and that your agreements cover them.

## The treatment center revenue cycle

### Admissions and VOB

The cycle starts before admission. VOB staff verify:

- active coverage and plan type;
- in- and out-of-network benefits by level of care;
- deductibles, coinsurance and out-of-pocket maximums;
- authorization and pre-certification requirements;
- day limits and step-down rules; and
- whether behavioral health is carved out.

Admissions staff need answers fast, often while a prospective patient is on the phone. Speed and accuracy both matter. See [eligibility verification and prior authorization](https://medicalbillingteam.com/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/).

### Utilization review support

Clinical staff conduct reviews, but billing and UR coordinators track authorization numbers, approved days, next review dates and denials, and make sure authorization data flows onto claims.

### Claims, denials and A/R

Common problems include authorization mismatches (dates or units on the claim not matching the authorization), wrong payer (carve-out not identified), missing documentation for level-of-care billing and timely filing. Our guides on [denial management](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/) and [reducing A/R days](https://medicalbillingteam.com/reduce-ar-days/) apply directly.

### Payment posting and reconciliation

Out-of-network claims, single-case agreements and patient responsibility make posting more complex. Accurate posting shows whether payers paid what was agreed.

## Mental health parity

Federal mental health parity rules generally require that limits on mental health and substance use disorder benefits be no more restrictive than those on medical and surgical benefits. The parity regulations and their enforcement have changed in recent years, so check current guidance from the Departments of Labor, HHS and the Treasury. Billing staff don't enforce parity, but recognizing patterns of more restrictive treatment can inform appeals. For specific parity questions, consult counsel.

## Staffing behavioral health billing

### Roles

- **VOB / admissions support specialist**
- **Authorization and concurrent review coordinator**
- **Behavioral health biller / claims specialist**
- **A/R and denial follow-up specialist**
- **Payment poster**

### What to look for

- Experience with behavioral health payers, carve-outs and levels of care
- Comfort working with admissions under time pressure
- Accurate tracking habits for authorizations and review dates
- Training on HIPAA, psychotherapy notes and Part 2
- Clear documentation of every payer interaction

### In-house, outsourced or remote?

- **In-house** works well when admissions and billing need constant face-to-face coordination.
- **Outsourced billing companies** that specialize in behavioral health can take the whole function; confirm how they handle VOB speed and Part 2.
- **Dedicated remote staff** can cover VOB, authorizations, claims and A/R in your systems, including evening and weekend admissions coverage if scheduled. Put a BAA and access controls in place first, and limit access to what each role needs ([HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/)).

Our operator, [Alliance Global Solutions](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/about-us/), provides remote staff including VOB and admissions support for treatment programs. If you're weighing options, request a [free staffing assessment](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/); we'll talk through your levels of care and payer mix. As always, please don't send patient information.

## Checklist for behavioral health billing leaders

- [ ] Authorization matrix by payer, level of care and service
- [ ] Concurrent review calendar with owner for each case
- [ ] Carve-out identification step in every eligibility check
- [ ] Psychotherapy notes excluded from billing staff access
- [ ] Part 2 consent tracking and staff training documented
- [ ] Authorization data validated against claims before submission
- [ ] Monthly denial review by payer and reason

A note on scope: this guide covers billing operations, not clinical or legal requirements. Licensure, program certification and state rules vary, so check them with your state agencies and counsel.

- [Eligibility verification and prior authorization](https://medicalbillingteam.com/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/)
- [HIPAA and outsourced billing staff](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/)
- [Revenue cycle management staffing (main guide)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/)
- [Prior authorization specialist role](https://medicalbillingteam.com/prior-authorization-specialist/)

## FAQ

### Why is behavioral health billing different from other specialties?

Behavioral health often involves time-based psychotherapy codes, frequent authorizations and concurrent reviews, levels of care with different benefits, carved-out behavioral health plans, and extra privacy rules for substance use disorder records under 42 CFR Part 2.

### What is a VOB in a treatment center?

A verification of benefits confirms a prospective patient's coverage and benefits for specific levels of care, such as detox, residential, partial hospitalization or intensive outpatient, including authorization requirements, day limits and out-of-network benefits, usually before admission.

### Does 42 CFR Part 2 apply to billing staff?

Part 2 applies to federally assisted SUD programs and to certain recipients of Part 2 records, including HIPAA covered entities and business associates and qualified service organizations. Billing staff who handle Part 2 records must follow its consent and redisclosure rules. HHS says compliance with the 2024 final rule was required by February 16, 2026.

### Can remote staff handle admissions and VOB for a treatment center?

Yes, VOB and admissions support are phone- and portal-based and can be done remotely, provided staff are trained on levels of care, coverage rules and privacy requirements, and work under a BAA with appropriate access controls.

### What should a behavioral health practice look for in billing staff?

Experience with behavioral health codes and payers, authorization and concurrent review tracking, knowledge of carve-out plans, understanding of Part 2 and psychotherapy notes rules, and strong documentation habits.

# What does an AR specialist do in medical billing?

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** An accounts receivable (A/R) specialist follows up on unpaid and underpaid insurance claims until they're paid, corrected, appealed or properly written off. The job is checking claim status, calling payers, fixing errors, documenting every action and escalating patterns. You need one, or more hours from one, when claims are aging past 60 to 90 days and nobody has time to work them.

Claims don't pay themselves. Some are lost, some are pended for information, some are underpaid and some are denied without anyone noticing. The A/R specialist is the person who finds them and pushes them to resolution. It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.

## A typical day

- **Work the queue.** Pull unpaid claims from the aging report, prioritized by dollar value and age, not alphabetically.
- **Check status.** Use payer portals and clearinghouse reports first, and call when the portal doesn't answer the question.
- **Fix and resubmit.** Correct demographic, coding or coordination-of-benefits errors, and send corrected claims.
- **Escalate denials.** Route denials to appeal or correction with the deadline noted (see [denial management basics](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/)).
- **Spot underpayments.** Compare payments with contracted rates and flag shortfalls.
- **Document everything.** Every touch gets a note: what was done, who was contacted, the reference number and the next follow-up date.

## Why the role matters

Unworked A/R gets harder to collect over time, and every payer has filing and appeal limits. For Medicare, the claim filing limit is one calendar year from the date of service ([CMS Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 1, §70](https://www.cms.gov/regulations-and-guidance/guidance/manuals/downloads/clm104c01.pdf)). Commercial payers often set shorter limits in their contracts. In a 2025 vendor survey of billing professionals, 26% named timely filing as a common denial reason ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)).

Denied claims also tend to stay denied when nobody follows up. KFF found consumers appealed fewer than 1% of denied in-network claims on HealthCare.gov plans in 2023 ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/private-insurance/claims-denials-and-appeals-in-aca-marketplace-plans-in-2023/)). That's patient-side data, but the lesson carries over: denials that no one works go unpaid.

## Skills to hire for

- Reading ERAs and EOBs, including CARC and RARC codes
- Payer portal navigation and efficient payer calls
- Knowledge of timely filing, corrected-claim and appeal rules for your main payers
- Your practice management system and clearinghouse
- Persistence, organization and clear notes
- Judgment about when to escalate (write-offs and refunds need approval)

## How to measure an AR specialist

Use measures you can see in your system:

- **Days in A/R** and the share of A/R over 90 days (see [how to reduce A/R days](https://medicalbillingteam.com/reduce-ar-days/))
- **Claims touched** per day, with notes and next-action dates
- **Dollars resolved:** paid, corrected or appealed
- **Aged A/R trend** by payer
- **Quality:** a sample of notes and actions reviewed each month

Avoid judging the role on claims touched alone. A day spent resolving one large, complicated claim can be worth more than 50 quick status checks.

## When to add an AR specialist

Signs you need more A/R capacity:

- A/R over 90 days is growing month over month.
- Claims are hitting timely filing limits.
- Your biller does A/R "when there's time," which is never.
- Denials sit unworked for weeks.
- You can't say what happened to a specific unpaid claim.

## In-house, outsourced or remote?

A/R follow-up is well suited to remote work because it happens in portals, on the phone and in your practice management system. Options include an in-house hire, a billing company that takes over A/R (often for a percentage of collections), or a dedicated remote specialist who works your queue in your systems. The [staffing cost guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-staffing-cost/) compares them. Whatever you choose, sign a BAA and set up role-based access first.

This site is operated by Alliance Global Solutions, which provides remote staff. You can read about its [remote medical billing staff](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/medical-billing/) or its [remote accounting staff](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/accounting/). For a second opinion on your A/R workload, request a [free staffing assessment](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/).

## Related guides

- [Revenue cycle management staffing (main guide)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/)
- [How to reduce A/R days](https://medicalbillingteam.com/reduce-ar-days/)
- [Prior authorization specialist role](https://medicalbillingteam.com/prior-authorization-specialist/)

## FAQ

### What is the difference between a medical biller and an AR specialist?

In smaller practices one person often does both. Billing focuses on getting clean claims out the door; A/R follow-up focuses on claims that were sent but not paid in full.

### How many claims should an AR specialist work per day?

It depends on claim complexity, payer mix and how much is done by portal versus phone. Set expectations after a few weeks of real data, and measure dollars resolved as well as claims touched.

### Can A/R follow-up be done remotely?

Yes. It happens in payer portals, by phone and in your practice management system. Remote staff need a BAA, secure access, and role-based permissions.

### What is the Medicare timely filing limit?

CMS sets it at one calendar year from the date of service. Commercial payer limits vary by contract and are often shorter.

### What KPIs should I track for A/R?

Days in A/R, the percentage of A/R over 90 days, dollars resolved, aged A/R by payer, and a quality review of documented actions.

# Hiring remote medical coders: what to verify, test and set up

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** Hire remote medical coders the way you'd hire local ones, then add security controls. Verify credentials directly with the issuing body, match specialty experience to your services, and give a practical coding test on fictional records. Agree on accuracy audits and turnaround, and put a BAA, MFA, secure remote access and role-based access in place before the coder sees a chart.

Coding sits between documentation and payment. A coder who doesn't know your specialty, or who works without quality checks, can create denials, compliance risk and rework. This guide covers what to look for in a remote or offshore coder and how to set up the role safely. It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) guide.

## What a medical coder does

Medical coders review clinical documentation and assign diagnosis and procedure codes: ICD-10-CM for diagnoses, and CPT and HCPCS for procedures, services and supplies. Typical tasks include:

- coding encounters, procedures or facility claims from provider documentation;
- applying modifiers and checking payer-specific coding rules;
- sending queries to providers when documentation is unclear or incomplete;
- working coding-related denials with the billing team; and
- keeping up with annual and quarterly code-set changes.

Code sets change on a schedule. CMS notes that ICD-10 code updates take effect on October 1 each year ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coding-billing/icd-10-codes)), and CPT is maintained by the AMA's CPT Editorial Panel ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/cpt/cpt-overview-and-code-approval)). Whoever codes for you needs a routine for updates.

## What it costs to hire locally

The Bureau of Labor Statistics groups coders with medical records specialists. It reports a median wage of $51,140 a year ($24.59 an hour) in May 2025 ([BLS](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/medical-records-and-health-information-technicians.htm)). Add benefits, which average 30% of private-industry compensation costs ([BLS](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ecec.nr0.htm)), plus software, training and management time. Our [staffing cost guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-staffing-cost/) has a worksheet for comparing that with remote options.

## Skills and credentials to verify

- **Credentials.** Recognized coding credentials from established certifying organizations. Verify them directly with the certifying body; don't rely on a résumé or a screenshot.
- **Specialty fit.** Professional (physician) coding differs from facility, ASC, behavioral health or therapy coding. Ask for experience in your services specifically.
- **Documentation literacy.** Can the coder spot when documentation doesn't support a code, and write a clear, compliant provider query?
- **Payer rules.** Modifier use, bundling edits and payer-specific policies.
- **Systems.** Your EHR and practice management system, encoder tools and any computer-assisted coding software you use.
- **Communication.** Clear written English for queries and notes.

## How to test a coding candidate

1. **Use fictional or de-identified sample notes.** Never use real patient records in a hiring test.
2. **Score accuracy, not speed alone.** Compare the candidate's codes with an answer key prepared by an experienced coder.
3. **Include one ambiguous case.** You're looking for a good provider query, not a guess.
4. **Include a denial.** Ask how they'd respond to a sample coding-related denial.

## Setting up the role

- **Scope.** Which encounter types, providers or locations, and what turnaround?
- **Quality program.** Agree on a regular audit sample, how errors are fed back, and what happens when accuracy drops. Many organizations audit new coders more heavily at first.
- **Query workflow.** How queries reach providers, how answers are documented, and who follows up.
- **Escalation.** Questions about compliance or medical necessity go to a named person in your organization.
- **Productivity.** Set expectations after a few weeks of real data, not before.

## Security and HIPAA for remote coders

Coders see full clinical documentation, so they're often the most PHI-exposed people on a billing team. Before access:

- a signed business associate agreement with the agency or contractor ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html));
- unique logins with MFA, and secure remote access through a virtual desktop or VPN;
- no local downloads, printing or USB storage;
- access limited to the charts and functions the role needs; and
- documented HIPAA training.

See our [HIPAA guide for outsourced billing staff](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/) for the full list of questions to ask. If you're considering offshore coders, read our guide to [offshore medical billers](https://medicalbillingteam.com/offshore-medical-billers/) for the extra checks.

## In-house, agency or freelancer?

A freelancer can cover a small, steady volume, but you handle vetting, backup coverage and security. An agency or staffing provider handles employment, equipment, backup coverage and the BAA, and adds a margin. A full-service billing company may include coding in a percentage-of-collections fee. Compare total cost and control, not just the hourly rate.

This site is operated by Alliance Global Solutions, which provides remote staff, including for coding-related roles. It signs a BAA with each client before any of its staff access protected health information. You can read about its [remote medical billing staff](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/medical-billing/) or [browse its virtual staff profiles](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistants/). To talk through your coding volume, request a [free staffing assessment](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/).

## Related guides

- [Revenue cycle management staffing (main guide)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/)
- [Hiring remote and offshore medical billers](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hire-remote-medical-billers/)
- [What an AR specialist does](https://medicalbillingteam.com/ar-specialist/)

## FAQ

### Do remote medical coders need certification?

No federal law requires a coding credential, but many employers and agencies require one from an established certifying organization. Verify any credential directly with the certifying body.

### How do I test a remote coder?

Give a practical test using fictional or de-identified notes, score accuracy against an answer key prepared by an experienced coder, and include an ambiguous case to see how the candidate writes a provider query.

### Can offshore coders code for US practices?

Yes, if they're trained in US code sets and payer rules, work under a BAA with strong access controls, and your payer and Medicaid contracts don't restrict offshore access to member data.

### How often should a coder's work be audited?

Agree on a regular audit sample with your coding lead. New coders are commonly audited more heavily at first, then on a routine schedule once accuracy is consistent.

### What does a medical coder earn in the US?

BLS reports a median of $51,140 a year ($24.59 an hour) in May 2025 for medical records specialists, the occupation group that includes coders.

# Prior authorization specialist: what the job involves and how to staff it

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** A prior authorization (PA) specialist gets payer approval before services that require it. The specialist checks requirements, gathers clinical documentation, submits requests, follows up, and tracks approvals, denials, expirations and visit limits. The workload is heavy: physicians in an AMA survey reported 39 PA requests per physician per week, and 40%% have staff who work exclusively on PA.

Prior authorization is one of the most time-consuming administrative tasks in a practice, and when it goes wrong it shows up as delayed care and denied claims. This guide covers what a PA specialist does, what changed under the CMS prior authorization rule, and how to staff the role. It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.

## How big the PA workload is

In an AMA survey of 1,000 physicians conducted in late 2024, physicians reported completing an average of 39 prior authorizations per physician per week. They and their staff spent about 13 hours a week on PA, and 40% said they have staff who work exclusively on it ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/fixing-prior-auth-nearly-40-prior-authorizations-week-way)). PA problems also drive denials: in a 2025 vendor survey of billing professionals, 31% cited prior authorization or referral issues as a common denial reason ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)).

## What a PA specialist does

1. **Identifies requirements.** Checks whether the service, drug or procedure needs authorization for the patient's specific plan.
2. **Gathers documentation.** Collects the clinical notes, test results and codes the payer requires, working with clinical staff.
3. **Submits the request** through the payer's portal, an electronic workflow, fax or phone.
4. **Follows up** on pending requests and responds to requests for more information.
5. **Records the outcome:** authorization number, approved units or visits, dates and any conditions.
6. **Handles denials:** routes them for peer-to-peer review or appeal, with deadlines noted.
7. **Tracks expirations and limits** so renewals go in before care is interrupted.

## What changed: CMS-0057-F

The CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F) applies to impacted payers, including Medicare Advantage organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP programs, and certain other plans. Under the rule, starting in 2026 these payers must send decisions within 72 hours for expedited requests and seven calendar days for standard requests, and must give a specific reason for denials. Payers must also build prior authorization APIs by January 1, 2027. The rule excludes drugs ([CMS fact sheet](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/cms-interoperability-and-prior-authorization-final-rule-cms-0057-f)).

Faster decisions help, but they don't remove the work of preparing complete requests, tracking them and acting on denials. Our [eligibility verification and prior authorization guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/) covers the full front-end workflow.

## Appeals are worth tracking

KFF data cited by the AMA shows that in 2023, Medicare Advantage enrollees or providers appealed only 11.7% of PA denials, but 81.7% of appeals were fully or partially overturned ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/fixing-prior-auth-nearly-40-prior-authorizations-week-way)). A PA specialist who flags appealable denials quickly, with the deadline, gives your clinicians the chance to act.

## Skills to hire for

- Knowledge of payer PA rules for your specialty and main payers
- Comfort reading clinical documentation and matching it to payer criteria
- Payer portal experience and organized follow-up
- Accurate tracking of authorization numbers, units and dates
- Clear communication with clinicians, front desk and billing
- Training on HIPAA and minimum necessary access, because PA involves clinical information

## Measuring the role

- Requests submitted, pending and resolved each week
- Average time from order to submission
- Approvals, denials and appeals, by payer
- Claims denied for missing or mismatched authorization (should trend down)
- Authorizations renewed before expiration

## Staffing options

PA work happens in portals, on the phone and in your EHR, so it can be done remotely. Options include in-house staff, a billing company that includes PA, or dedicated remote specialists working your queue. For high-volume specialties and treatment centers, a dedicated PA person often frees front-desk and clinical time (see our [behavioral health billing guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/behavioral-health-billing/)). Sign a BAA and set role-based access before any remote specialist sees clinical records ([HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/)).

This site is operated by Alliance Global Solutions, which provides remote staff. You can read about its [medical billing staff](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/medical-billing/) or its [call center and customer service staff](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/call-center-customer-service/), who handle phone-heavy work. To talk through PA volume, request a [free staffing assessment](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/).

## Related guides

- [Revenue cycle management staffing (main guide)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/)
- [Credentialing specialist role](https://medicalbillingteam.com/credentialing-specialist/)
- [What an AR specialist does](https://medicalbillingteam.com/ar-specialist/)

## FAQ

### What does a prior authorization specialist do?

Checks whether services need payer approval, gathers documentation, submits requests, follows up, records approvals and tracks expirations, and routes denials for peer-to-peer review or appeal.

### How many prior authorizations do practices handle?

Physicians in an AMA survey conducted in late 2024 reported an average of 39 prior authorizations per physician per week, with about 13 hours of physician and staff time spent on them.

### What are the CMS-0057-F decision timeframes?

For impacted payers, decisions within 72 hours for expedited requests and seven calendar days for standard requests, plus a specific reason for denials. Drugs are excluded.

### Can prior authorization be done remotely?

Yes. The work happens in payer portals, by phone and in the EHR. Remote staff need a BAA, secure access, role-based permissions and HIPAA training.

### Are prior authorization denials worth appealing?

Often. KFF data cited by the AMA shows 81.7%% of Medicare Advantage PA denials that were appealed in 2023 were fully or partially overturned, though only 11.7%% were appealed.

# Credentialing specialist: what the role covers and how to staff it

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** A credentialing specialist gets providers approved, or "credentialed," and enrolled with insurance payers, and keeps them enrolled. That means gathering licenses and documents, keeping provider profiles current, submitting applications, following up until the effective date is confirmed, and tracking re-credentialing deadlines. Until enrollment is complete, claims for that provider may be denied or delayed.

Credentialing problems don't show up as a billing error until claims start denying. A new provider who starts seeing patients before payer enrollment is finished, or an expired license nobody tracked, can stall payment for weeks. This guide covers the credentialing workflow and how practices and billing companies staff it. It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.

## Credentialing vs enrollment

People use the terms interchangeably, but they're different steps:

- **Credentialing** verifies a provider's qualifications: education, training, licenses, board certification, work history, malpractice coverage and sanctions history.
- **Payer enrollment** gets the provider added to a payer's network or program so claims can be paid, with a confirmed effective date.

Hospitals and facilities also run their own credentialing and privileging. That's a separate process, though many specialists handle both.

## The workflow

1. **Collect documents.** Licenses, DEA registration where applicable, board certification, malpractice insurance, CV and work history, and identifiers such as the NPI.
2. **Maintain provider profiles.** Many commercial payers use a shared credentialing database that providers must keep current and re-attest periodically. Medicare and Medicaid have their own enrollment systems.
3. **Submit applications** to each payer, following that payer's process.
4. **Follow up.** Track every application with a date submitted, a reference number, the payer contact and the next follow-up date. Applications stall without follow-up.
5. **Confirm effective dates and contracts.** Make sure the provider is linked to the right group, tax ID and locations, and that billing knows the effective date.
6. **Track expirations and re-credentialing.** Licenses, malpractice policies, DEA registrations and payer re-credentialing cycles all expire on different schedules.

## What slows credentialing down

- Incomplete or inconsistent applications (addresses, practice locations, dates)
- Profiles not re-attested on time
- Missing malpractice or license documents
- Applications submitted late, after the provider has already started
- No follow-up after submission
- Billing not told the effective date, so claims go out too early or too late

Timelines vary widely by payer, state and application type, so plan well ahead of a provider's start date. Ask each payer for current processing expectations rather than relying on a general number.

## A simple credentialing tracker

Even a spreadsheet works if it is kept current. For each provider and payer, track: application type, date submitted, reference number, payer contact, current status, next follow-up date, effective date once approved, and the re-credentialing due date. Add a separate tab for expirations (licenses, DEA, malpractice, board certification) with reminders 90 and 30 days out. Review the tracker weekly with practice leadership, and tell billing the moment an effective date is confirmed.

## Skills to hire for

- Organization and deadline tracking across many payers and providers
- Experience with payer enrollment portals and shared credentialing databases
- Accuracy with detail-heavy forms
- Persistent, documented follow-up
- Coordination with providers, billing and practice leadership

## Staffing credentialing

Credentialing workload is lumpy. It spikes when you add providers, locations or payers, then settles into maintenance. Options:

- **In-house:** works when you hire often and want control. The risk is that it lands on an office manager with no time.
- **Credentialing service or billing company:** often priced per provider or per application.
- **Dedicated remote specialist:** works in your portals and tracker, part-time or full-time. This is useful for billing companies that credential for many clients.

Credentialing files include sensitive provider information (such as Social Security numbers and license details), so require secure access and clear data-handling rules whichever option you choose. If remote staff will also see patient data, sign a BAA first ([HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/)).

Front-end steps such as [prior authorization](https://medicalbillingteam.com/prior-authorization-specialist/) and [eligibility verification](https://medicalbillingteam.com/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/) depend on providers being correctly enrolled, so connect credentialing to those teams.

This site is operated by Alliance Global Solutions, which provides remote staff. You can read about its [administrative virtual assistants](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/administrative/) or its [medical billing staffing services](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/medical-billing/). To talk through credentialing support, request a [free staffing assessment](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/).

## Related guides

- [Revenue cycle management staffing (main guide)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/)
- [Prior authorization specialist role](https://medicalbillingteam.com/prior-authorization-specialist/)
- [Virtual medical assistants for billing and front office](https://medicalbillingteam.com/virtual-medical-assistant/)

## FAQ

### What is the difference between credentialing and payer enrollment?

Credentialing verifies a provider's qualifications. Enrollment adds the provider to a payer's network or program with an effective date, so claims can be paid.

### How long does credentialing take?

It varies widely by payer, state and application type. Start well before a provider's first day and ask each payer for its current processing expectations.

### What documents does a credentialing specialist need?

Typically licenses, DEA registration where applicable, board certification, malpractice insurance, CV and work history, and identifiers such as the NPI.

### Can credentialing be done remotely?

Yes. Most work happens in payer portals, credentialing databases and email. Require secure access and clear data-handling rules because the files contain sensitive provider information.

### Why do claims deny for credentialing reasons?

Common causes are a provider not yet enrolled with the payer, a wrong effective date, or the provider not linked to the correct group, tax ID or location.

# Virtual medical assistants for billing and front-office work

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** A virtual medical assistant is a remote staff member who handles administrative work for a practice, such as eligibility checks, prior authorization follow-up, appointment reminders, data entry, payment posting and inbox management. A virtual assistant is not a clinical medical assistant and shouldn't do clinical tasks. Because the role touches patient data, require a BAA and secure access before day one.

"Virtual medical assistant" is a broad term. In practice it usually means remote administrative help for an overloaded front desk or billing team. This guide covers what a virtual assistant can and can't do, how the role fits with billing, and how to set it up safely. It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.

## What a virtual medical assistant can do

**Front-office and scheduling support**
- Appointment confirmations and reminder calls
- Insurance card and demographic updates in the practice management system
- Referral and records-request tracking
- Inbox, fax and portal message triage (non-clinical routing)

**Billing-adjacent work**
- Eligibility and benefits checks before visits (see [eligibility verification](https://medicalbillingteam.com/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/))
- Prior authorization submissions and follow-up (see [prior authorization specialist](https://medicalbillingteam.com/prior-authorization-specialist/))
- Charge entry from structured encounter forms
- Payment posting support and simple reconciliation
- Patient statement questions and payment plan setup, following your scripts

**Practice admin**
- Credentialing paperwork and expiration tracking (see [credentialing specialist](https://medicalbillingteam.com/credentialing-specialist/))
- Report preparation and data cleanup

## What to keep in-house or with licensed staff

- Clinical tasks, triage, medical advice or anything that requires a license
- In-person work: check-in, collecting payments, rooming patients
- Decisions on write-offs, refunds and policy exceptions (the assistant can prepare them, but a manager approves)

Medical assistants in a clinic are a different occupation with clinical duties; a virtual administrative assistant isn't a substitute for that role.

## Why practices use virtual assistants

Administrative load is a major pressure on small practices. Prior authorization alone accounted for about 13 hours a week of physician and staff time in an AMA survey ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/fixing-prior-auth-nearly-40-prior-authorizations-week-way)). Hiring is also hard: in a 2025 vendor survey, 38% of billing professionals said they struggle to find qualified candidates ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)). A virtual assistant can take repeatable administrative tasks off the front desk so in-office staff can focus on patients.

## Virtual assistant or dedicated biller?

| If your biggest problem is... | Consider |
|---|---|
| Phones, reminders, eligibility and paperwork | A virtual medical assistant |
| Unworked A/R and denials | A dedicated [AR specialist](https://medicalbillingteam.com/ar-specialist/) |
| Claims going out late or with errors | A dedicated remote biller |
| All of the above | A small team with defined queues |

## HIPAA and security setup

A virtual assistant who sees schedules, insurance information or billing records handles PHI. Before day one:

- sign a BAA with the staffing provider or contractor ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html));
- create unique logins with MFA, and use secure remote access through a virtual desktop or VPN;
- grant only the access the tasks require (minimum necessary);
- block local downloads, printing and personal devices; and
- train on HIPAA and your policies, and keep records.

There's no official "HIPAA certified" virtual assistant. See our [HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/) for the safeguards to ask about.

## How to start

1. **List the tasks** that eat the most front-desk and billing time each week.
2. **Write simple procedures** for the first two or three tasks, with scripts for patient calls.
3. **Start with a defined schedule** that overlaps your office hours.
4. **Check in daily** for the first two weeks, then weekly.
5. **Measure:** tasks completed, eligibility checked before visits, PA turnaround, and errors caught.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- **Handing over everything at once.** Start with two or three tasks and add more as procedures settle.
- **No written procedures.** Assistants can only follow the process you've written down; undocumented "tribal knowledge" leads to errors.
- **Shared logins.** Every person needs their own account so access can be audited and removed.
- **No single point of contact.** Name one person in the office who answers the assistant's questions and reviews their work.

This site is operated by Alliance Global Solutions, which provides remote staff. It signs a BAA with each client before any of its staff access protected health information. You can read about its [administrative virtual assistants](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/administrative/) or [browse virtual staff profiles](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistants/). To talk through which tasks to hand off, request a [free staffing assessment](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/).

## Related guides

- [Revenue cycle management staffing (main guide)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/)
- [Prior authorization specialist role](https://medicalbillingteam.com/prior-authorization-specialist/)
- [Credentialing specialist role](https://medicalbillingteam.com/credentialing-specialist/)

## FAQ

### What does a virtual medical assistant do?

Remote administrative work such as appointment reminders, eligibility checks, prior authorization follow-up, data and charge entry, payment posting support, and inbox and fax triage.

### Can a virtual medical assistant do clinical tasks?

No. Virtual administrative assistants shouldn't perform clinical tasks, triage or give medical advice. Keep those with licensed, in-person staff.

### Is a virtual medical assistant HIPAA compliant?

A virtual assistant can work within HIPAA when there's a BAA, secure access, minimum necessary permissions and training. There is no official HIPAA certification for assistants or companies.

### How is a virtual medical assistant different from a medical biller?

A virtual assistant handles broad administrative tasks; a biller focuses on claims, A/R and denials. Many small practices start with an assistant and add billing capacity later.

### How do I start with a virtual medical assistant?

List the most time-consuming administrative tasks, write procedures for two or three of them, agree on a schedule, sign a BAA, and check in daily for the first two weeks.

# Medical billing outsourcing: three models and how to choose

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** There are three main ways to outsource medical billing. A full-service billing company runs the whole function, usually for a percentage of collections. A staffing model gives you dedicated remote billers who work in your systems under your direction. A hybrid outsources specific queues, such as A/R or prior authorization. The right choice depends on how much control you want, your volume and your specialty.

"Outsourcing medical billing" can mean very different arrangements. Comparing a percentage-of-collections billing company with a dedicated remote biller is like comparing a managed service with a hire. This guide lays out the models so you can compare them fairly. It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.

## Model 1: Full-service billing company

The billing company takes over most or all of the revenue cycle: charge entry, claims, payment posting, A/R, denials and often patient statements. It usually works in its own software or yours.

- **Typical pricing:** a percentage of collections, a per-claim fee or a flat monthly fee
- **Good fit:** practices that want billing off their plate entirely
- **Watch for:** less visibility into day-to-day work, contract terms that make leaving hard, unclear ownership of data and reports, and fees on collections the practice would have received anyway

## Model 2: Dedicated remote staff (staffing model)

A staffing provider recruits and employs billers who work only on your account, in your systems, following your procedures. You direct the work; the provider handles employment, equipment, backup coverage and HR.

- **Typical pricing:** a monthly or hourly rate per full-time person
- **Good fit:** practices and billing companies that want control and visibility, and have someone to direct the work
- **Watch for:** you still need management time and documented procedures; quality depends on hiring and training

## Model 3: Hybrid

Keep billing in-house and outsource specific queues: A/R follow-up, denials, eligibility, prior authorization or credentialing. This works well when one area is chronically behind.

- **Typical pricing:** per person, per task or per queue
- **Good fit:** practices with a capable in-house biller who is overloaded
- **Watch for:** clear handoffs between teams so nothing falls through the gaps

## How to compare the models

| Factor | Billing company | Dedicated remote staff | Hybrid |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who directs the work | Vendor | You | Both |
| Software | Vendor's or yours | Yours | Yours |
| Pricing basis | % of collections or per claim | Per person | Per person or task |
| Visibility | Vendor reports | Your queues and reports | Mixed |
| Management time needed | Low | Medium | Medium |
| Exit difficulty | Contract-dependent | Usually simpler | Usually simpler |

Run your own numbers with the worksheet in our [staffing cost guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-staffing-cost/). It uses public BLS wage and benefit data for the in-house baseline.

## Questions to ask any outsourcing partner

1. Who exactly will work on our account, and where are they located?
2. Will you sign a business associate agreement, and do your subcontractors sign one too?
3. What access controls do you use (MFA, secure remote access, no local downloads)?
4. What reports will we get, and can we see the work queues directly?
5. How are errors, write-offs and refunds approved?
6. What happens to our data and reports if we end the relationship?
7. What are the contract term, notice period and fees for leaving?
8. Can you give references we can contact directly?

Be cautious of anyone who promises a specific reduction in denials or A/R days before reviewing your data. Results depend on your payers, specialty and processes.

## HIPAA applies to every model

Any outsourcing partner whose people access patient information on your behalf is generally a business associate under HIPAA, and you need a BAA before access ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)). There is no official "HIPAA certification" for vendors. Ask about specific safeguards instead, using our [HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/). If the team is overseas, read our guide to [offshore medical billers](https://medicalbillingteam.com/offshore-medical-billers/).

## Which model fits?

- **Small practice, no billing manager, wants it handled:** a billing company is often simplest.
- **Practice or billing company with a manager and growing volume:** dedicated remote staff gives capacity with control.
- **Strong in-house biller, one area behind:** hybrid.

This site is operated by Alliance Global Solutions, which offers the dedicated-staff model. It signs a BAA with each client before any of its staff access protected health information. You can read about its [outsourced medical billing staffing](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/medical-billing/) and broader [staffing services](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/services/). If you'd like help deciding, request a [free staffing assessment](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/); we'll tell you if a billing company is the better fit.

## Related guides

- [Revenue cycle management staffing (main guide)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/)
- [Offshore medical billers: pros, cons and safeguards](https://medicalbillingteam.com/offshore-medical-billers/)
- [Hiring remote and offshore medical billers](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hire-remote-medical-billers/)

## FAQ

### What does it cost to outsource medical billing?

Billing companies commonly charge a percentage of collections, per claim or a flat fee. Dedicated remote staff are usually priced per full-time person. Compare total cost, including your management time, with a worksheet.

### Is outsourcing medical billing HIPAA compliant?

It can be, when the partner signs a BAA and uses appropriate safeguards. HIPAA compliance depends on contracts and practices, not a certification; there is no official HIPAA certification.

### What is the difference between a billing company and a staffing model?

A billing company runs the function and directs the work. With a staffing model, dedicated remote billers work in your systems under your direction.

### Can I outsource only part of my billing?

Yes. A hybrid model outsources specific queues such as A/R follow-up, denials, eligibility, prior authorization or credentialing.

### Will outsourcing reduce my denials?

It depends on your payers, specialty, documentation and processes. Be cautious of promises of a specific reduction made before anyone reviews your data.

# Offshore medical billers: pros, cons and the safeguards to require

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** Offshore medical billers can add capacity at a lower hourly cost than local hires, and many practices and billing companies use them for A/R follow-up, eligibility, payment posting and denials. HIPAA doesn't ban offshore work, but HHS notes that overseas arrangements can raise risk and enforceability questions. Check your payer and Medicaid contracts, require a BAA and strong access controls, and include offshore access in your risk analysis.

Offshore billing teams are common in US healthcare, and they're also a source of understandable worry about data security, quality and communication. This guide covers where offshore billers fit, the real risks and the safeguards to require. It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.

## Why practices and billing companies go offshore

- **Hiring difficulty.** In a 2025 vendor survey, 38% of billing professionals said they struggle to find qualified candidates, and 28% cited unaffordable wages ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)).
- **Cost structure.** US billing and posting clerks had a median wage of $23.32 an hour in May 2025 ([BLS](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ocwage.t01.htm)), before benefits, which average 30% of private-industry compensation costs ([BLS](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ecec.nr0.htm)). Offshore staff are typically priced lower per hour, but compare total cost with our [staffing cost worksheet](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-staffing-cost/).
- **Coverage.** A dedicated offshore person can keep queues moving when local staff are out, and some schedules cover hours your office doesn't.

## Work that suits offshore billers

- A/R follow-up and claim status checks
- Eligibility and benefits verification
- Payment posting and reconciliation
- Denial follow-up and corrected claims
- Charge entry from structured source documents
- Prior authorization submissions and follow-up (see [prior authorization specialist](https://medicalbillingteam.com/prior-authorization-specialist/))

Work that needs physical presence, such as front-desk check-in, collecting payments in person or handling paper mail, stays local.

## The risks, honestly

- **Data security.** Offshore staff access PHI from outside the US. HHS's cloud computing guidance notes that HIPAA doesn't prohibit storing or processing PHI overseas, but that doing so may raise the risks to the data and can make legal enforcement harder; covered entities should consider these risks in their risk analysis ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html)).
- **Contract restrictions.** Some payer contracts, state Medicaid programs and government plans restrict offshore access to member data. Check yours before you start.
- **Quality and communication.** Billing depends on payer-specific knowledge and clear notes. Poor hiring or training shows up quickly in denials.
- **Time zones.** Payer phone lines keep US hours. Confirm schedules in writing.

## Safeguards to require

1. **Business associate agreement** with the provider before any access, and subcontractor BAAs where applicable ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)).
2. **Unique logins and MFA** on every system.
3. **Secure remote access** through a virtual desktop or VPN, so PHI stays in your environment.
4. **No local downloads, printing, screenshots or USB storage**, technically enforced where possible.
5. **Company-managed, encrypted devices** and secured work locations.
6. **Role-based, minimum necessary access**, removed the same day someone leaves.
7. **HIPAA training** at onboarding and annually, with records.
8. **Background checks** and a clear acceptable-use policy.
9. **Incident response** with a defined, prompt notification timeline. Under HIPAA, a business associate must notify the covered entity of a breach without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/breach-notification/index.html)). Many contracts set a shorter window.

And remember there's no official "HIPAA certification." Ask for evidence of the safeguards above instead. Our [HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/) has 15 questions to ask.

## Start small

Start with one well-defined queue, such as eligibility or A/R follow-up, with written procedures and daily spot checks. Review results after 30 days before expanding. Our guide to [hiring remote medical billers](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hire-remote-medical-billers/) includes interview questions and a 30-day onboarding plan.

## Offshore vs nearshore vs US remote

| | Offshore | Nearshore | US remote |
|---|---|---|---|
| Typical hourly cost | Lowest | Middle | Highest |
| Time-zone overlap | Needs scheduling | Good | Full |
| Contract restrictions | Check carefully | Check | Usually fewer |
| HIPAA safeguards needed | Same, plus overseas risk analysis | Same, plus cross-border review | Same |

This site is operated by [Alliance Global Solutions](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/about-us/), which provides remote staff based in the Philippines. It signs a BAA with each client before any of its staff access protected health information. You can read about its [offshore medical billing staff](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/medical-billing/). If you're weighing an offshore team, request a [free staffing assessment](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/); we'll also tell you when it isn't a fit.

## Related guides

- [Revenue cycle management staffing (main guide)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/)
- [Medical billing outsourcing: three models](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-outsourcing/)
- [Hiring remote medical coders](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hire-remote-medical-coders/)

## FAQ

### Is offshore medical billing legal under HIPAA?

HIPAA doesn't prohibit offshore work. HHS notes overseas arrangements may raise risk and enforcement challenges, so include them in your risk analysis, sign a BAA and check payer and Medicaid contracts for restrictions.

### What billing tasks can offshore staff do?

Common tasks include A/R follow-up, eligibility verification, payment posting, denial follow-up, charge entry and prior authorization submissions.

### How do offshore billers keep PHI secure?

Through a BAA, unique logins with MFA, secure remote access via virtual desktop or VPN, no local downloads or printing, managed encrypted devices, role-based access, training and incident response.

### Do offshore billers work US hours?

Many teams work schedules that overlap US business hours so they can call payers. Confirm the schedule in writing.

### Are offshore medical billers HIPAA certified?

No one is. There is no official HIPAA certification; HHS does not certify vendors. Ask for evidence of specific safeguards instead.

# How a remote medical billing team works

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** You tell us which billing work needs help. Alliance Global Solutions recruits dedicated remote staff for those roles, and they work in your systems, under your workflows, once a business associate agreement and access controls are in place. You direct the work; the staffing provider employs and supports the staff.

A dedicated remote billing team is people, not software. Here is what the process looks like from the first conversation to day-to-day work.

## Step 1: Tell us about your workload

Use the [short form on the home page](https://medicalbillingteam.com/#assessment) or the [longer contact form](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/). We ask for practice-level details only: specialty, number of providers, a collections range and your current setup. **Never include patient information.**

## Step 2: Free staffing assessment

A billing staffing specialist talks with you, usually for 20 to 30 minutes, about:

- which queues are falling behind (eligibility, authorizations, claims, denials, A/R, posting);
- your systems, payers and specialty-specific rules;
- whether your systems can support secure remote access;
- the hours and coverage you need; and
- whether a remote team is a sensible fit at all.

If it isn't, for example because your processes are undocumented or your payer contracts restrict offshore access, we'll tell you.

## Step 3: Meet candidates, sign agreements, onboard

If you decide to go ahead:

1. **Role definition.** We agree on tasks, hours, systems and how performance will be measured.
2. **Candidate interviews.** You interview shortlisted candidates and choose who joins your team.
3. **Agreements.** A services agreement and a **business associate agreement (BAA)** are signed before anyone receives access to protected health information. See our [HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/).
4. **Secure access setup.** Unique logins, multi-factor authentication, role-based permissions and secure remote access (VDI or VPN), with no local downloads.
5. **Training on your workflows.** Your procedures, payers, escalation rules and reporting.
6. **Ramp-up.** Start with a defined queue, review work closely in the first weeks, then expand.

## Day to day

- Staff work your queues during agreed hours, often overlapping US business hours.
- You set priorities and approve anything outside the agreed rules (write-offs, refunds, appeals strategy).
- You get regular reporting on volumes worked and the KPIs you choose, such as days in A/R or denial rate. See [RCM KPIs, defined](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/).
- You can add roles or reduce capacity under the terms of your agreement.

## What we don't do

- We don't ask for patient information through this website.
- We don't claim to be "HIPAA certified"; no such official certification exists.
- We don't promise specific outcomes before understanding your data.

## FAQ

### Do remote staff use our software or theirs?

Yours. Dedicated staff work in your practice management system, clearinghouse and payer portals, with access you grant and can revoke at any time.

### Who manages the remote staff day to day?

You direct the work and set priorities. The staffing provider handles employment, HR, equipment, attendance and support, and can help with supervision and reporting.

### What do we need to have in place first?

A signed business associate agreement, a secure way for staff to reach your systems (ideally a virtual desktop or VPN with MFA), user accounts with role-based access, and documented procedures for the tasks you're assigning.

### Can we start with one person?

Yes. Many practices start with one role, such as eligibility verification or A/R follow-up, and add more once the workflow is running smoothly.

# Frequently asked questions

## About remote billing staff

### What is a remote medical billing team?

Dedicated billing and revenue cycle staff who work remotely in your systems, under your workflows. You direct the work; a staffing provider recruits, employs and supports the staff. [How it works →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/how-it-works/)

### How is a staffing model different from outsourcing to a billing company?

A billing company usually takes over the billing function, often for a percentage of collections. With a staffing model you get dedicated people working your queues in your software, and you keep control of the process and payer relationships. [Cost comparison →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-staffing-cost/)

### What roles can remote staff cover?

Common roles include billing and claims specialists, A/R follow-up, denial follow-up, eligibility and benefits verification (VOB), prior authorization, payment posting, coding (with credentials), credentialing and admissions or intake support. [RCM staffing guide →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/)

### Do you work with medical billing companies?

Yes. Billing companies often add dedicated remote staff as they take on new clients.

## HIPAA and security

### Is anyone 'HIPAA certified'?

No. There is no official HIPAA certification for companies or individuals. HHS's Office for Civil Rights does not endorse or certify vendors. Ask about specific safeguards instead: a BAA, MFA, secure remote access, role-based access, training and incident response. Source: [HHS, cloud computing guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html). [HIPAA guide →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/)

### Will the staffing provider sign a business associate agreement?

A provider whose staff will access protected health information on your behalf is generally a business associate, and a BAA should be signed before any access. Have your counsel review it. Alliance Global Solutions signs a business associate agreement (BAA) with each client before any of its staff access protected health information. Source: [HHS, business associates](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html).

### Is offshore billing allowed under HIPAA?

HIPAA does not ban offshore work, but HHS notes that overseas arrangements can increase risk and raise enforceability questions. Address them in your risk analysis, and check payer and Medicaid contracts, some of which restrict offshore access.

## Cost and results

We don't publish generic price ranges. [Cost worksheet →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-staffing-cost/)

### Can you guarantee lower denials or fewer A/R days?

No. Results depend on your payers, specialty, documentation and processes. Anyone promising a specific reduction before reviewing your data should be asked how they can know that.

## Getting started

### What hours do remote staff work?

Schedules are agreed up front. Many teams overlap US business hours so they can call payers and handle same-day eligibility work.

Yes. Many practices start with one queue, such as eligibility or A/R follow-up, and expand once it runs smoothly.

## How we write our guides

- **We explain options fairly**, including when in-house staff or a full-service billing company is a better fit than remote staff.
- **We cite public sources.** Any statistic on this site links to a public source such as CMS, HHS, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the AMA or KFF. Where we cite a vendor survey, we say so. If we can't find a reliable public source for a number, we leave the number out.
- **We don't promise results.** Billing outcomes depend on your payers, specialty, documentation and processes. We don't claim that any staffing model will cut denials or A/R days by a set amount.
- **No fake proof.** You won't find invented testimonials, star ratings, client logos or case studies here. If we ever publish a client story, it will be real, permission-based and clearly labeled.
- **We are not "HIPAA certified," and neither is anyone else.** There is no official HIPAA certification. We explain what safeguards to look for in our [HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/).
- **Dates mean something.** Each guide shows its original publication date and the date of its last substantive update. We change the "Updated" date only when content meaningfully changes, not for a redesign or rebuild. Guides are reviewed at least quarterly and whenever CMS, HHS, payers or code sets change something they cover.
- **Who writes and reviews.** Guides are published under the Medical Billing Team editors byline. We don't invent author personas or credentials. When a named reviewer with medical billing experience checks a guide, their name and role will appear on it.
- **How we use automation.** We use AI tools to help research and draft. Every statistic and regulatory statement is checked against the linked public source before publishing, and the sources are linked inline.

## Not legal or financial advice

Our content is general information. It is not legal, compliance, coding or financial advice. For decisions about HIPAA, contracts or reimbursement, talk to qualified advisers.

## Your information

Our forms collect only business contact and practice-level information. **Please never submit patient information.** We explain what we collect and how we use it in our [Privacy Policy](https://medicalbillingteam.com/privacy/).

## Contact

Questions or corrections? [Contact us](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/). If you spot an error in a guide, we want to fix it.

## Related domain

medicalbillingadvisor.com is a related domain. Once its redirect is set up, it will point to this site.
